segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now the apostles and the brothers and sisters throughout Judea heard that the Gentiles too had received the word of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when Peter went up to Jerusalem, the circumcised believers took issue with him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You went in to uncircumcised men and ate with them.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Peter began and laid it all out for them in order, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision: something like a large sheet coming down, lowered from heaven by its four corners, and it came right up to me.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: I stared at it and looked closely, and I saw the four-footed animals of the earth, the wild beasts, the crawling things, and the birds of the sky.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: I also heard a voice saying to me, ‘Get up, Peter; slaughter and eat.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But I said, ‘Certainly not, Lord, for nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But a voice answered a second time from heaven, ‘What God has made clean, you must not treat as common.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: This happened three times, and then everything was pulled up again into heaven.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And at that very moment three men arrived at the house where we were, sent to me from Caesarea.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: The Spirit told me to go with them, making no distinction. These six brothers also came with me, and we entered the man’s house.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: He reported to us how he had seen the angel standing in his house and saying, ‘Send to Joppa and summon Simon, who is called Peter;

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: he will speak words to you by which you will be saved, you and all your household.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And I remembered the word of the Lord, how he used to say, ‘John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So if God gave them the same gift he gave us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could hinder God?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they heard this, they fell silent. Then they glorified God, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “So then, God has given even to the Gentiles the turning back that leads to life.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now those who had been scattered by the affliction that arose over Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except Jews.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But some of them, men from Cyprus and Cyrene, came to Antioch and began to speak to the Greek speakers as well, announcing the good news of the Lord Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number who believed turned to the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The report about them reached the ears of the assembly in Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas out as far as Antioch.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he arrived and saw the grace of God, he rejoiced, and he urged them all to remain true to the Lord with resolute hearts,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. And a large crowd was added to the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he went off to Tarsus to look for Saul,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and when he found him he brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they gathered with the assembly and taught a large crowd, and it was in Antioch that the disciples were first called Christians.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In those days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: One of them, named Agabus, stood up and indicated through the Spirit that a great famine was about to come over the whole inhabited world—and this took place under Claudius.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the disciples decided, each according to their means, to send relief to the brothers and sisters living in Judea.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This they did, sending it to the elders by the hand of Barnabas and Saul.

notes.note: The Greek word means “nations” or “peoples.” Jewish writers used its plural for all the peoples other than Israel. This translation renders the same word “Gentiles” where non-Jews are meant and “nations” where peoples as such are in view.

notes.traditional: they that were of the circumcision
notes.note: Literally “those of circumcision.” The phrase may mean simply Jewish believers, which at this point is nearly everyone in the Jerusalem community. It may instead mean a group within it that insisted on circumcision and separation from Gentiles. The Greek does not settle which.

The word ordinarily meant “shared” or “ordinary.” Jewish Greek used it for what is ritually profane, such as food unfit for a people set apart to God. The verb in verse 9, “treat as common,” is built on the same word, so the voice turns Peter’s own term back on him.

The same verb can mean “hesitate” or “doubt,” and many translations render it so here, matching the parallel at 10:20. The form here is active, which favors “making no distinction,” that is, between Jew and Gentile. The same verb is translated “took issue” in verse 2, so Peter’s critics are doing what the Spirit told him not to do. Manuscripts vary in the wording of this phrase.

Most translations keep “repentance,” understood to include a change of life. In current English, “repentance” centers on feeling sorry. The Greek word carries the prophets’ call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct.

Most translations have “persecution” here, which fits the events of chapter 8. The Greek is the general word for hardship pressing on people from outside, and this translation renders it “affliction” throughout so the reader can see it is one word.

Manuscripts are divided between “Hellenists” (Greek speakers), the reading translated here, and the plain word “Greeks.” In 6:1 the first word refers to Greek-speaking Jews. Here the contrast with “Jews” in verse 19 shows that non-Jews are meant on either reading, and most scholars agree on that sense.
Older translations have “preaching the Lord Jesus.” The verb was an ordinary word for announcing good news publicly. Many modern translations also render it “good news” here.

“Church” is the near-universal rendering, and readers know what it refers to. A first-century hearer knew the word as a civic gathering of citizens and as the Greek Old Testament’s term for Israel assembled before God. “Church” now suggests a building or an institution, so this translation uses “assembly” wherever the word occurs.

The name is formed the way party labels were formed, meaning roughly “Christ’s people” or “partisans of Christ.” The verb can mean to bear a name publicly. Most scholars think outsiders in Antioch coined the label, though this is not certain. The word is rare in the New Testament, appearing elsewhere only at Acts 26:28 and 1 Peter 4:16.

The term means the inhabited world and was often used loosely for the Roman Empire. Claudius was emperor from AD 41 to 54. Ancient sources record repeated food shortages during his reign, including a severe famine in Judea in the mid-40s.

candidates.reason: The plural for community members recurs throughout Acts and the letters, and translators split between “brothers,” “brothers and sisters,” and “believers.” Here “brothers” is kept in verse 12, where six specific men are meant.
It occurs at Acts 6:1, 9:29 and 11:20 with different referents, and English versions vary between “Hellenists,” “Grecians,” “Greeks,” and paraphrases.
The ritual sense (with κοινόω) recurs in Mark 7, Acts 10–11, Romans 14 and Hebrews, and versions vary between “common,” “profane,” “impure,” and “defiled.”
It recurs in Luke–Acts, Hebrews and Revelation, where “world,” “inhabited world,” and “empire” are all defensible and should be distinguished from κόσμος.

candidates.rendering: take issue with (middle) / make a distinction (active)
candidates.reason: The verb’s range across “dispute,” “distinguish,” and “doubt/hesitate” recurs in Acts, Romans, 1 Corinthians and James, and wordplay is lost if the renderings are chosen ad hoc.
